title: Fine-tuning & Training
description: When to fine-tune, building datasets, LoRA/QLoRA, quantization and preference tuning, then a tuned model you can compare and serve

mustKnow.oneLiner: Prompt first, add retrieval for changing facts, fine-tune for stable style, format or behaviour.
mustKnow.misconception: Fine-tuning is the way to teach a model new facts.

mustKnow.oneLiner: Supervised training on prompt-and-reply pairs so the model follows your format and tone.
mustKnow.misconception: You need thousands of examples; a few hundred clean ones can shift behaviour.

mustKnow.oneLiner: Freeze the base model and train small low-rank adapters, about 1% of the parameters or fewer.
mustKnow.misconception: LoRA is a lower-quality shortcut; on most tasks it is close to full fine-tuning.

mustKnow.oneLiner: LoRA on top of a 4-bit quantized frozen base, so a 7-8B model trains on one consumer GPU.
mustKnow.misconception: The adapter is trained in 4-bit; only the frozen base is quantized.

mustKnow.oneLiner: Store weights in fewer bits to save memory and speed up inference, at some quality cost.
mustKnow.misconception: Quantization is free; always re-run your eval.

mustKnow.oneLiner: Hold out examples the model never sees; duplicates across the split inflate your scores.
mustKnow.misconception: Low training loss means the model is good.

mustKnow.oneLiner: Preference and reward-based tuning after SFT: DPO uses chosen/rejected pairs; GRPO with verifiable rewards uses checkable answers.
mustKnow.misconception: You need RL to get a useful tuned model; SFT alone is often enough.

stageGoals.beginner: Decide whether a task needs fine-tuning, and build a clean, validated 200-example chat dataset with a fixed-seed train/eval split.
stageGoals.intermediate: Run a QLoRA fine-tune of a small open model in free Colab and show how it compares with a well-prompted baseline on a held-out set.
stageGoals.advanced: Merge, quantize and serve the tuned model locally, and measure the quality, speed and memory cost of each quantization level.

startHere: If you already fine-tuned a model with PEFT, skim c401 to c404 and start at c405; if you only prompt today, start at c401 and do the dataset project early.
outcomes: Decide between prompting, RAG and fine-tuning for a given NuraKnect task and explain the trade-off
Build, clean, validate and split a chat-format instruction dataset
Fine-tune a small open model with QLoRA in free Colab using one training stack
Compare a tuned model with a prompted baseline on a held-out eval set
Quantize a model to GGUF and serve it locally while measuring the quality cost
Explain where DPO and GRPO fit after supervised fine-tuning

evidence: A cleaned 200-example dataset with a data card and a reproducible split

quiz.unlockCondition: Complete all core items in this layer

questions.question: Your NuraKnect assistant must answer in your brand voice and also quote current prices. Which parts would you fine-tune, and which would you leave to retrieval or prompts? Defend the split.
questions.hint: Style and format are learned behaviours; prices change and need a source of truth.

questions.question: Design the data flow from raw Instagram DMs to a train/eval split you trust. Where do privacy, dedupe and leakage get handled?
questions.hint: Think about anonymising before anything is stored, dedupe before splitting and splitting by conversation.

questions.question: Your LoRA run's training loss falls nicely but the tuned model is no better than the prompted base on eval. List three things you would check first.
questions.hint: Eval set quality, overfitting, data that does not match the target behaviour, learning rate and epochs.

questions.question: You must serve the tuned model on a 16 GB laptop. Walk through the steps from adapter to running endpoint and the checks you would run after quantizing.
questions.hint: Merge, convert to GGUF, pick a quant level, rerun the same eval and compare latency and memory.

questions.question: A teammate says the model needs to know your latest product catalogue. What is the best first approach?
questions.hint: Choose the approach that keeps facts easy to update.
options: Fine-tune on the catalogue every week
Retrieve catalogue entries at query time
Train a new model from scratch
Raise the temperature setting
questions.explanation: Facts that change belong in retrieval (RAG), where you can update the source without retraining. Fine-tuning is better for style, format and behaviour.

questions.question: Why do you keep a held-out eval set that the model never trains on?
questions.hint: Think about what a training score can and cannot tell you.
options: It makes training run faster
It lowers the memory needed
It lets you use a larger learning rate
It measures performance on unseen examples
questions.explanation: Only unseen examples show whether the model generalises. Scores on training data hide memorisation and overfitting.

questions.question: In LoRA, a layer with d_in 4096, d_out 4096 and rank r=8 trains how many parameters?
questions.explanation: LoRA trains A (r x d_in) and B (d_out x r): 8 * (4096 + 4096) = 65,536 parameters, instead of the 16,777,216 in the full matrix.

questions.question: What does QLoRA add on top of plain LoRA?
questions.hint: It is about how the frozen base weights are stored.
options: Fully trains every layer in 4-bit
A reward model for preference data
A 4-bit quantized frozen base model
A larger adapter rank by default
questions.explanation: QLoRA keeps the frozen base model in 4-bit (NF4) and trains LoRA adapters on top, which cuts memory enough for a free Colab GPU.

questions.question: Which data does DPO need?
questions.hint: It learns from comparisons, not single answers.
options: Only unlabeled raw text
Prompts with chosen and rejected replies
A separate trained reward model's outputs only
Unit tests that grade each answer
questions.explanation: DPO trains directly on preference pairs: a prompt with a chosen and a rejected reply. It removes the separate reward model that classic RLHF needs.

questions.question: You quantize a tuned model from fp16 to 4-bit to run it locally. What should you do next?
questions.hint: Compression is a trade-off you must measure.
options: Assume quality is unchanged
Retrain the model from scratch
Delete the original fp16 weights
Re-run your eval and compare with fp16
questions.explanation: Quantization trades quality for size and speed, and the loss varies by model and task. Re-run the same eval to measure it before shipping.

pythonChallenge.title: Validate a JSONL Chat Dataset
pythonChallenge.question:
Fine-tuning data is only as good as its format. Most trainers (OpenAI, TRL, Unsloth) expect one JSON object per line, shaped like {"messages": [{"role": ..., "content": ...}, ...]}. A single bad line can crash a run an hour in.

Your task:
Write  validate_line(line)  that takes ONE line of a JSONL file (a string) and returns a list of error strings. An empty list means the line is valid.

A line is valid when:
  1. It parses as JSON and is an object with a non-empty "messages" list
  2. Every message is an object with role in {"system", "user", "assistant"} and a non-empty string "content"
  3. At least one message has role "user"
  4. The LAST message has role "assistant" (that is the reply the model learns to produce)

Then write  validate_file(lines)  that returns {line_number: [errors]} (line numbers start at 1) for the invalid lines only.

Try it on a few NuraKnect-style DM examples, including a broken one.
pythonChallenge.hint: Return early with one error when json.loads fails. After that, collect all the rule violations into the list instead of stopping at the first one.
pythonChallenge.starterCode:
import json

VALID_ROLES = {"system", "user", "assistant"}

def validate_line(line):
    errors = []
    # TODO: parse JSON (return ["invalid json"] on failure)
    # TODO: check "messages" is a non-empty list
    # TODO: check each message role and content
    # TODO: check there is a user message and the last message is from the assistant
    return errors

def validate_file(lines):
    # TODO: return {line_number: errors} for invalid lines only (numbers start at 1)
    return {}

good = '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Do you ship to Canada?"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Yes, 5-7 days."}]}'
print(validate_line(good))
pythonChallenge.tests:
assert validate_line('{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "hello"}]}') == [], "a valid line should return []"
assert len(validate_line("not json")) >= 1, "broken JSON should produce an error"
assert len(validate_line('{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}')) >= 1, "last message must be from the assistant"
assert len(validate_line('{"messages": [{"role": "robot", "content": "hi"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "x"}]}')) >= 1, "unknown role should be rejected"
assert len(validate_line('{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "  "}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "x"}]}')) >= 1, "empty content should be rejected"
assert list(validate_file(['{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "a"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "b"}]}', "oops"]).keys()) == [2], "validate_file should report only line 2"
hints: json.loads raises json.JSONDecodeError (a ValueError) on bad input.
Use isinstance(x, list) and isinstance(m, dict) checks before indexing so a wrong shape gives an error, not a crash.
validate_file: loop with enumerate(lines, start=1), call validate_line, keep the entry only if the result is non-empty.

courses.title: AI Engineering from Scratch: Data Pipelines (Phase 10, lesson 03)
courses.why: Dataset quality decides the result. This lesson covers cleaning, dedupe, filtering and splits, which is the exact work of turning NuraKnect DMs into training data.

pythonChallenge.title: Dedupe and Split with a Fixed Seed
pythonChallenge.question:
Duplicate examples are the quiet killer of fine-tuning evals: if the same DM appears in train and eval, your score is inflated and you will not notice. You also need the split to be reproducible so a re-run gives the same eval set.

Your task:
Write  dedupe_and_split(examples, eval_fraction=0.2, seed=42)  where examples is a list of dicts {"prompt": str, "reply": str}.

  1. Remove duplicates by normalised prompt (lowercase, strip, collapse repeated whitespace). Keep the FIRST occurrence.
  2. Shuffle the unique examples with  random.Random(seed)  (do not touch the global random state and do not mutate the input list).
  3. eval size = max(1, round(n * eval_fraction)) where n is the unique count.
  4. Return (train, eval) as two lists.

The same input and seed must always give the same split, and no prompt may appear in both lists.
pythonChallenge.hint: Build a seen set of normalised prompts while looping. Normalise with ' '.join(text.lower().split()). Copy the list before shuffling.
pythonChallenge.starterCode:
import random

def normalise(text):
    # TODO: lowercase, strip and collapse whitespace
    return text

def dedupe_and_split(examples, eval_fraction=0.2, seed=42):
    # TODO: 1) dedupe by normalised prompt, keep the first
    # TODO: 2) shuffle a copy with random.Random(seed)
    # TODO: 3) eval size = max(1, round(n * eval_fraction))
    train, held_out = [], []
    return train, held_out

data = [{"prompt": f"Question {i}", "reply": f"Answer {i}"} for i in range(10)]
data += [{"prompt": "  question 3 ", "reply": "dup"}, {"prompt": "QUESTION   4", "reply": "dup"}]
train, held_out = dedupe_and_split(data)
print(len(train), len(held_out))
pythonChallenge.tests:
_data = [{"prompt": f"Question {i}", "reply": f"Answer {i}"} for i in range(10)] + [{"prompt": "  question 3 ", "reply": "dup"}, {"prompt": "QUESTION   4", "reply": "dup"}]
_copy = list(_data)
_tr, _ev = dedupe_and_split(_data)
assert len(_tr) + len(_ev) == 10, "duplicates (after normalising) should be removed, leaving 10 unique examples"
assert len(_ev) == 2, "eval size should be round(10 * 0.2) = 2"
assert dedupe_and_split(_data) == (_tr, _ev), "the same seed must give the same split"
assert not ({normalise(e["prompt"]) for e in _tr} & {normalise(e["prompt"]) for e in _ev}), "no prompt may appear in both train and eval"
assert _data == _copy, "do not mutate the input list"
assert len(dedupe_and_split(_data[:3], eval_fraction=0.01)[1]) == 1, "eval should have at least 1 example"
hints: Loop over examples; if normalise(e['prompt']) is already in seen, skip it, otherwise add it and append e to unique.
n_eval = max(1, round(len(items) * eval_fraction)); return items[n_eval:], items[:n_eval]

pythonChallenge.title: LoRA Parameter-Count Calculator
pythonChallenge.question:
LoRA freezes a weight matrix W (d_out x d_in) and trains two small matrices instead: A (r x d_in) and B (d_out x r). So one adapted layer trains  r * (d_in + d_out)  parameters instead of  d_in * d_out.

Your task:
  1. Write  lora_params(d_in, d_out, r)  returning the trainable parameters for ONE adapted layer.
  2. Write  lora_report(layers, r)  where layers is a list of (d_in, d_out) tuples. Return a dict with keys:
       "lora"    : total LoRA parameters across all layers
       "full"    : total parameters if you trained those layers fully
       "percent" : lora / full * 100

Sanity check from the lesson: a 4096 x 4096 layer at r=16 trains 131,072 parameters, about 0.78% of 16,777,216.
pythonChallenge.hint: Sum r * (d_in + d_out) over the layers for 'lora' and d_in * d_out for 'full'. Guard against an empty layers list (full == 0).
pythonChallenge.tests:
assert lora_params(4096, 4096, 16) == 131072, "4096x4096 at r=16 should be 131072"
assert lora_params(4096, 1024, 8) == 8 * (4096 + 1024), "use r * (d_in + d_out)"
_rep = lora_report([(4096, 4096)] * 4, 16)
assert _rep["lora"] == 4 * 131072, "lora total should sum over layers"
assert _rep["full"] == 4 * 4096 * 4096, "full total should be d_in * d_out per layer"
assert abs(_rep["percent"] - 0.78125) < 1e-6, "percent should be lora / full * 100"
assert lora_report([], 8)["percent"] == 0.0, "an empty layer list should not crash"
hints: A has r * d_in parameters and B has d_out * r parameters.
Use sum() with a generator over layers for each total.
percent = lora / full * 100 if full else 0.0

pythonChallenge.title: int8 Quantize and Dequantize
pythonChallenge.question:
Quantization stores weights in fewer bits to save memory. The simplest scheme is symmetric int8: pick one scale so the largest absolute value maps to 127, round every value to an integer, and multiply back by the scale to recover an approximation.

Your task:
  1. quantize_int8(values) returns (q, scale) where scale = max(abs(values)) / 127 (use scale 1.0 if all values are 0) and q[i] = round(values[i] / scale), clamped to the range -127..127.
  2. dequantize_int8(q, scale) returns [x * scale for x in q].
  3. max_error(values) returns the largest absolute difference between the original values and the round-tripped ones.

Try it on [0.5, -1.2, 3.3, 0.01] and see how the tiny value suffers.
pythonChallenge.hint: Python's round() works here. The biggest possible error per value is scale / 2, because rounding moves a value at most half a step.
pythonChallenge.tests:
_q, _s = quantize_int8([1.0, -1.0, 0.5])
assert _q[0] == 127 and _q[1] == -127, "the largest magnitude should map to +/-127"
assert abs(_s - 1.0 / 127) < 1e-9, "scale should be max(abs) / 127"
assert quantize_int8([0.0, 0.0]) == ([0, 0], 1.0), "all zeros should use scale 1.0"
assert all(-127 <= v <= 127 for v in quantize_int8([5.0, -9.0, 2.5])[0]), "q must stay inside -127..127"
assert len(dequantize_int8(*quantize_int8([0.5, -1.2]))) == 2, "dequantize should return one value per input"
_vals = [0.5, -1.2, 3.3, 0.01]
assert max_error(_vals) <= (3.3 / 127) / 2 + 1e-9, "error can never exceed scale / 2"
hints: max(abs(v) for v in values) gives the largest magnitude.
max_error: q, s = quantize_int8(values); back = dequantize_int8(q, s); return max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(values, back))
